Consider a decreasing sequence of \(n\) positive integers \(x_1 \gt x_2 \gt \cdots \gt x_n\) that satisfies the following two conditions:
• The average (arithmetic mean) of the first \(3\) terms in the sequence is \(2025.\)
• For all \(4 \le k \le n,\) the average of the first \(k\) terms in the sequence is \(1\) less than the average of the first \(k-1\) terms in the sequence.
What is the greatest possible value of \(n?\)

statement.html: A rectangular grid of squares has \(141\) rows and \(91\) columns. Each square has room for two numbers. Horace and Vera each fill in the grid by putting the numbers from \(1\) through \(141 \times 91 = 12{,}831\) into the squares. Horace fills the grid horizontally: he puts \(1\) through \(91\) in order from left to right into row \(1,\) puts \(92\) through \(182\) into row \(2\) in order from left to right, and continues similarly through row \(141.\) Vera fills the grid vertically: she puts \(1\) through \(141\) in order from top to bottom into column \(1,\) then \(142\) through \(282\) into column \(2\) in order from top to bottom, and continues similarly through column \(91.\) How many squares get two copies of the same number?

statement.html:
A frog hops along the number line according to the following rules.
• It starts at \(0.\)
• If it is at \(0,\) then it moves to \(1\) with probability \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) and it disappears with probability \(\dfrac{1}{2}.\)
• For \(n = 1,\) \(2,\) or \(3,\) if it is at \(n,\) then it moves to \(n+1\) with probability \(\dfrac{1}{4},\) it moves to \(n-1\) with probability \(\dfrac{1}{4},\) and it disappears with probability \(\dfrac{1}{2}.\)
What is the probability that the frog reaches \(4?\)
